title: How are linear representations learned? Exact solutions to the dynamics of abstraction
claim: A minimal solvable setting with concept geometry and a noise direction captures nontrivial, non-monotonic abstraction dynamics that prior theories miss.
layout: 5 panels: 3D schematics on top, two line plots and kernel matrix below
description: The top row has two 3D-style schematics, A and B, with a central legend. Each shows red and blue circles and squares joined by colored arrows for the shape, color and interaction directions, plus the concept vectors u_red and u_blue. In A the red and blue shape vectors are parallel, which is perfect abstraction. In B a green orthogonal 'noise' axis tilts them apart. The bottom row has two line plots and a matrix. Panel C plots shape abstraction against training epoch for a ConvNet. It spikes, dips negative, then plateaus near 0.6. Panel D overlays abstraction (blue), probe test error (orange) and a dotted theory curve. Panel E is a 4x4 block kernel with shaded blocks labeled a_d, a_2, a_1s, a_1c and a_0. The eye goes first to the colorful schematics.
caption: Problem setting (see §2 for more details). We consider a minimal solvable setting with two binary concepts (shape, color) giving us four classes C := { , , , }. (A) Schematic of perfectly abstract representation where shape concept vectors ured and ublue have cosine similarity αshape = 1. (B) In the minimal model, introducing an orthogonal interaction mode (SC, green) with eigenvalue λSC lowers the abstraction αshape, hence we refer to it as the “noise” direction. (C) The abstraction trajectory of a deep ConvNet trained on the 3dshapes dataset [21] exhibits nontrivial dynamics, which is not captured by prior theories. In particular, its trajectory is non-monotonic and it plateaus well below α = 1 (see §D.2.2 for experiment details). In this paper, our aim is a dynamical theory of abstraction which captures such behavior. (D) Abstraction and probe generalization of deep ReLU network trained on synthetic data (see §D.1.1 for experimental details). P red→blue
abstract: In artificial and biological neural networks, concepts are often encoded as consistent linear directions in representation space. In deep learning, this idea is known as the linear representation hypothesis and underpins many interpretability and control methods based on linear probes, from concept detection to activation steering. Yet while prior work has studied whether such directions should exist $\textit{after}$ training, the dynamics of how they emerge $\textit{during}$ training remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a framework to study the alignment of concept directions during training - a process we call "abstraction". In a minimal linear network setting, we obtain exact solutions for the full trajectory of abstraction. These solutions reveal key analytic principles governing abstraction: (i) data and target geometry jointly determine abstraction at the end-of-learning, (ii) abstraction improves with network depth, and (iii) initialization scale controls the maximum abstraction reached during training. Extending our theory to nonlinear networks, we analyze how the choice of nonlinearity affects abstraction dynamics: erf networks approximate the linear theory, while abstraction in ReLU networks depends less on target geometry and more on input geometry. Across both, we prove a striking attenuation law: both nonlinearities weaken abstraction in activations relative to preactivations. We find evidence for this law in open models (DINOv3, Gemma 4) and apply our theory to improve linear probe generalization in LLMs. Together, our results provide a dynamical theory of abstraction with implications for interpretability and control.
